To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the free energy per monomeric unit of a protein aggregate depends on the number of participating units and that this dependence is non-linear.

the free energy change DeltaDeltaG of protein aggregation varies with the number n of participating monomers and that the free energy reaches a maximum for n=2, and that DeltaDeltaG(1) < DeltaDeltaG(3) < DeltaDelta(G2) for the aggregation of U1A.

1) the free energy per monomers DeltaDeltaG(n) is negative for n = 1 and n = 3; 2) the free energy is positive for n = 4; 3) the free energy reaches a maximum for n=2; 4) DeltaDeltaG(3) is negative; 5) the free energy of a trimer relative to the monomer is DeltaDeltaG(1) + DeltaDeltaG(4) = -3
In summary, our research is concerned with
protein aggregation and protein folding in the context of the nucleolus.
the thermodynamic properties of protein aggregation.
the thermodynamics of protein aggregation and the development of new methods to quantitate the thermodynamic parameters of the process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the U1A dimer is more stable than the U1A trimer by 3 kT.
the dimeric aggregate is stabilized by 3.1 kJ/mol relative to the monomer, while the trimer is stabilized by 0.4 kJ/mol relative the dimer.
the free energy per monomeric subunit of the U1A trimer is lower than that of the dimer, and that the dimer is stabilized by the tethers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the free energy per monomers is lowest in the trimer, intermediate in the dimer, and highest in the monomer.
the free energy per monomers of the aggregate is a minimum for the dimer, and increases for larger aggregates.
a binary aggregate is favored over a trimer, and that a trimer is favored over a monomer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the free energy per monomeric unit of a protein aggregate can be quantitated in a single experiment, by linking the protein into a series of oligomeric constructs.
the free energy per monomeric unit of an aggregate can be quantified with high precision by using tethers.

the free energy landscape of protein aggregation can be quantitated with great precision by tethering the protein into dimers and/or trimers, and measuring the kinetics of aggregation in the presence of these tethers.
